title: The Secret of Whisperwind Falls
markdown:
Glen liked his days to be smooth, like a well-worn pebble. His goats, a woolly bleating flock, were the happiest in the valley, and that was not luck. He knew which kid wanted the sunny patch and which ewe wanted the shade, often before the goat knew it herself. The emerald hills rolled around his pasture like a green sea that never quite reached the gate.

One dewy morning he was checking on Bartholomew, his prize-winning billy, a magnificent creature with horns like polished oak branches. Beneath a loose stone near the pasture gate he found a small folded paper, scribbled in berry juice the colour of deep twilight.

A tiny flutter caught his eye. Nori the notebook fairy landed on the stone, wings like brittle autumn pages. She collected observations, not coins. Her leather-bound notebook already held the shapes of clouds, the taste of raindrops on her tongue, and the way a spider’s web shimmered like a dropped necklace in the morning sun.

"What is this, Glen?" Her voice was dry leaves in a gentle breeze.

He unfolded the paper. A wobbly arrow pointed toward the Whisperwind Mountains. Beneath it, three words in the same juice: Waterfall. Before dawn.

A tight knot formed in his chest. His fingers felt clumsy as he smoothed the paper. He pictured his best woollen socks, the ones his grandmother had knitted, thoroughly soaked. "Before dawn? That is awfully early. The sun hardly bothers to show its face then. And waterfalls. They are always rather damp."

Nori clapped her tiny hands, page-wings fluttering. "A mystery. A treasure hunt. The colours of the sky before the sun. The sound of the water in the quiet. Magnificent notes."

Glen sighed, a sound like wind through dry reeds, but Nori’s enthusiasm was as infectious as a spring meadow in full bloom. "All right. Extra dry socks. And a good waterproof cloak."

They set off while the moon was still a sliver of silver and the world was hushed. Glen checked Bartholomew’s gate twice, then a third time, because leaving a prize billy before dawn felt like leaving a sentence unfinished. The path wound upward through wet ferns that brushed his cloak. The air grew cooler with every step. A soft steady rumble, like a distant drumbeat, began to reach them.

"We are getting close," Nori chirped, barely audible above a roar that promised power and wildness.

They arrived at the base of Whisperwind Waterfall as the first pale grey smudged the eastern sky, a painter testing a brush. Water tumbled down the rocky face in a shimmering frothy curtain. Cool damp mist kissed their faces. A low resonant hum vibrated through the stone under their feet, blending with wet earth and moss.

Nori had her notebook open already and dipped a quill into a tiny inkpot. "Look. The water is so fine it floats. The air feels cooler here. As if the water is breathing the heat away."

Glen stood a little further back, dampness clinging to his cloak, surprising coolness settling on his skin. "The air is much nicer when it has been through the spray. Lighter. Fresher." He was thinking how the water seemed to disappear into the air, a shy whisper that vanished as soon as you tried to grasp it.

Then a mischievous gust snatched the paper from his hand and swallowed it into the swirling mist. His heart sank. The tremor in his stomach came back stronger. "The clue is gone. Completely vanished. We will never find the next part. I knew this was a bad idea. We should have stayed in our warm beds."

The damp cold rock near the fall felt like a bad omen. But Nori was watching the water, emerald eyes taking in the air and the rocks, not only the roar. He could not turn back only because it was damp and confusing.

"It is not gone," she said, as steady as the fall itself. "It has changed. Like the water turns into mist and then disappears. It is a part of the waterfall now." She pointed to a smooth moss-covered rock that seemed to absorb the spray without being washed away. "The clue spoke of the waterfall and the coolness. Look closer. Really look."

He stepped nearer, boots sinking slightly into damp earth. Spray kissed his face and banished some of the unease. The rock was dark and wet, slick with moisture, but etched into its surface, almost hidden, were faint lines. The same kind of scribbles as the clue, familiar and yet new.

Nori fluttered down. Her fingers, no bigger than pine needles, traced the lines with exquisite care. "A riddle. Where the breath of the mountain cools the air, a secret waits, beyond compare." She looked up, shining. "You were right. The water evaporating is what makes it cool. That is what the clue was telling us."

Glen looked from the damp rock, now a map of old marks, to the misty air still alive with the waterfall’s breath. A slow dawning spread across his face. Warmth chased the last of the knot. "So the clue was not lost. It was hidden in plain sight, showing us what was happening all along. We just needed to watch, and to listen."

The sun began to peek over the distant peaks, painting the swirling mist gold and rose. The waterfall roared its mighty song. Glen and Nori stood together, a sturdy goat herder and a diligent notebook fairy, bathed in a dawn they had walked toward on purpose. Bartholomew would still be waiting by the gate, horns like oak, and Glen’s extra socks, for once, were only a little damp.
